papers.title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

papers.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
papers.abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

papers.title: DriftGuard: Online Memory-Drift Detection via Causal Attribution for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on persistent memory to plan tool calls and complete multi-step tasks, which exposes them to memory drift: an adversarial or misleading memory alters the execution path and final outcome. In this work, we investigate online memory-drift detection, which estimates each retrieved memory's causal contribution to potential drift at serving time. We identify two fundamental challenges. (1) Content-level features are insufficient for causal memory-drift attribution, as perplexity or retrieval relevance alone cannot determine which retrieved memory would change agent behavior if neutralized; (2) Counterfactual attribution is prohibitively expensive for online detection, as it requires replaying downstream agent and tool execution for each candidate memory, exceeding real-time serving budgets. To address these challenges, we propose DriftGuard, a two-stage framework that decouples offline causal supervision from online estimation. Specifically, DriftGuard first constructs causal supervision through repeated paired counterfactual replays, continuing the original and single-memory neutralized trajectory suffixes from a shared pre-action state. The resulting annotations are aggregated by component-wise majority voting into a memory drift score (MDS) that captures action change, attack removal, violation removal, and task recovery. Guided by this supervision, DriftGuard then learns an online risk model that estimates MDS from pre-action information and flags drift-inducing memories via its maximum component risk, without online counterfactual rollouts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DriftGuard accurately identifies drift-inducing memories and enables efficient online defense. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DriftGuard-7F0B.

papers.title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
papers.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

papers.title: MambaLIFT: Reference-Based Mechanism-Aware Attribution for VMamba
papers.abstract: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models remains challenging because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways. We introduce MambaLIFT, a reference-based, multiplier-first attribution framework for VMamba that propagates contributions through its computational graph using interaction-aware rules for selective-scan injection, recurrent memory, LayerNorm, and shared pathways. MambaLIFT decomposes the reference-relative class-logit difference, \(f_c(x)-f_c(x^0)\), by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and computational mechanism. Experiments on ImageNet-1K evaluate VMamba-T and VMamba-B, with hyperparameters selected on a calibration set and faithfulness assessed on a disjoint held-out evaluation set. MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision across audited attribution interfaces in both configurations. Under mean-colour pixel flipping, it achieves significantly higher mean faithfulness scores than MambaLRP on both configurations and the highest scores among the evaluated methods, including Integrated Gradients with matched references. Under blurred replacement, MambaLIFT is non-inferior to MambaLRP on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B, indicating that its advantage depends on the replacement protocol. Ablations on VMamba-T show that interaction allocation, temporal propagation, and pathway composition affect attribution maps. Mechanism-level analyses further show that exact relevance conservation does not imply additive effects under finite interventions: the mechanism decomposition accounts for the reference-relative logit difference but does not estimate intervention effects or establish causal validity.

papers.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
papers.abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.

papers.title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
papers.abstract: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

papers.title: RouterWeave: A Unified Observation Layer for Cross-Platform Activity Analysis via Home Routers
papers.abstract: Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software integrations connect and control supported devices, yet vendor restrictions and licensing barriers limit access to their data, while hardware constraints hinder integration. Our key insight is that encrypted network traffic provides complementary evidence of activity across platform boundaries. Accordingly, we present RouterWeave, a router-side observation framework that combines cross-platform traffic collection, task-adaptive processing, and unified activity records. These records preserve activity meaning, temporal extent, and source-device attribution while distinguishing discrete operations from sustained activity intervals. We evaluate RouterWeave across four datasets, native execution on a commodity home router, and two novel case studies: cross-platform Screen Time monitoring and appliance energy estimation. RouterWeave achieves 94.41% macro-F1 on application activities and 97.46% on IoT operations, outperforming baselines by up to 20.99 percentage points, while using under 7 MB of router memory per task and supporting 54 concurrent devices within a 5-second update window. In end-to-end case studies, RouterWeave reconstructs 600 Screen Time timelines across Android, iOS, and Windows with 92.15% accuracy (24.84-second mean active-time error over 19-minute averages) and recovers 49 of 55 appliance operations over four days, tracking ON/OFF states with 92.84% agreement and estimating electricity use within a 4.28% error. Together, these results establish the commodity home router as practical infrastructure for whole-home activity sensing. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/naisslab/routerweave.

papers.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
papers.abstract: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

papers.title: User Perceptions of Deceptive In-Vehicle Infotainment User Interfaces
papers.abstract: Modern vehicles collect extensive data about drivers, passengers, and vehicle use, with privacy and consent decisions increasingly mediated through infotainment software. Although dark patterns have been widely studied in web, mobile, and e-commerce interfaces, little is known about how they appear in automotive infotainment systems or how users perceive them. We study this problem through Android Automotive OS (AAOS), conducting a three-phase empirical analysis. First, 26 HCI and privacy annotators audit four OEM AAOS emulators (Honda, Volvo, GM, and Polestar), documenting 17 dark-pattern types across 65 observations. Second, a user study with 100 participants compares OEM-specific implementations of five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo, finding that implementation choices affect user perceptions. Third, an independent study with 49 participants compares automotive and e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a brief tutorial, showing that automotive's initial rating advantage largely collapses after instruction. Together, the studies identify a sophistication paradox: subtler dark patterns are less likely to trigger user suspicion and may therefore be harder to identify. These findings indicate that oversight should evaluate not just the presence but also the specific implementation of dark patterns.

papers.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
papers.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

papers.title: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

papers.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

papers.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

papers.title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
papers.abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.

papers.title: Passing NPCR Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, a Detection Benchmark and an Audit of Published Image Ciphers
papers.abstract: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies. After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.

papers.title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
papers.abstract: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $π(a\mid x,m)$.

papers.title: MetaScanner: An Empirical Study and Proactive Defense against Deceptive UI Attacks in Social VR
papers.abstract: Social virtual reality (VR) platforms have surged in popularity but continue to face significant security challenges, including privacy invasion and user manipulation. Yet, the security risks posed by deceptive content remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce four novel deceptive UI attacks that covertly manipulate social VR users into performing unintended actions without their awareness. We show how adversarial content creators can embed seemingly benign scripts and interactive elements within carefully designed virtual worlds, deceiving users into unknowingly carrying out harmful behaviors. We implemented these attacks on VRChat, a leading social VR platform, and an IRB-approved user study involving 30 participants confirmed their effectiveness. To mitigate these threats, we propose MetaScanner, a proactive analysis system that efficiently scans virtual world assets, including scripts and interactive objects, to identify suspicious or deceptive elements before users are exposed to them. We demonstrate that MetaScanner can successfully detect all threats in test worlds where the four attack scenarios were implemented. Additionally, MetaScanner shows its lightweight nature, with an average scanning time of 5 seconds across 38 real-world assets.

papers.title: DNA: Unlocking Depth Scaling in CTR Models
papers.abstract: Long user behavior sequences are among the strongest signals for click-through rate (CTR) prediction. Cross-attention makes these sequences practical for industrial ranking by keeping compute linear in sequence length. Yet the gains from stacking cross-attention layers taper off: on Taobao search, growing a cross-attention stack from 16 to 28 layers adds only 0.02 percentage points (pt) of AUC. We argue that the key-value side is the bottleneck. Each layer projects the same behavior sequence into keys and values, so adding depth gives the model more reads of a fixed sequence. We propose DNA (Dual-stream Nexus Attention), which lets the sequence itself evolve with depth. At each layer, the request representation (the search query, user features and scene) first reads the sequence. Each behavior token then attends to the updated request representation and uses what it reads to update itself, so the next layer reads a sequence shaped by the current request. The update runs once per request, all candidates share the resulting sequence, and both the reads and the update keep linear complexity in sequence length. At comparable forward FLOPs, DNA improves AUC over cross-attention stacks by 0.08 to 0.26 pt and keeps improving in the depth range where those stacks level off. DNA-4 is deployed in Taobao search. In an online A/B test against the production model, it improves CTR by 0.8% and GMV by 0.5%.

papers.title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

papers.title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
papers.abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.

papers.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

papers.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

papers.title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
papers.abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

papers.title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
papers.abstract: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.

papers.title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.

papers.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

papers.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
papers.abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.

papers.title: LQ-Rec: Late Quantization for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) for sequential recommendation compresses each item into a short semantic ID and trains an autoregressive decoder to generate next-item codes from a user history. While appealing for cold-start handling and storage, au- toregressive GR suffers a structural scaling limit: typically, longer semantic IDs reduce quantization error in principle but degrade ranking quality and quadratic memory usage against semantic ID length. We propose Late Quantization (LQ), a non-autoregressive paradigm that confines discretization to the output (item) side of the pipeline. The encoder and scoring rule operate in continuous space, while items are stored and matched as semantic IDs produced by an end-to-end-trained residual quantizer. This architectural shift permits an additive error decomposition and a pairwise ordering theorem that jointly bound the quantization- induced ranking drop, a structural guarantee absent in prior semantic-ID recommenders. Across four public benchmarks, the resulting recommender, LQ-Rec, delivers three capabilities simultaneously: ranking quality improves monotonically with the semantic-ID length and outperforms existing baselines; a single trained model supports anytime compression, tuning ranking quality against inference cost without retraining; and LQ-Rec shows superior generalization on a memorization/generalization partition.

papers.title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
papers.abstract: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.

papers.title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
papers.abstract: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.

papers.title: Uncontrolled source titles: When Nature, Science, and PNAS meet Scopus
papers.abstract: Bibliographic databases such as Scopus and Web of Science play a critical role in literature discovery, systematic reviews, bibliometric analyses, and research evaluation, yet their reliability depends on effective control of the quality of the bibliographic data. This study examines the problem of uncontrolled source titles in Scopus by comparing five possibly adopted journal-level retrieval strategies across three flagship journals-Nature, Science, and PNAS. Substantial discrepancies across retrieval results indicate persistent fragmentation in the source title field. A comparative analysis using the Web of Science Core Collection shows that no comparable degree of uncontrolled source-title variation is observed for the same journals. The study further explores possible mechanisms, including inheritance of different title forms from (different) upstream providers, automated parsing and OCR-related artifacts, and insufficient cross-validation. Based on these findings, the study proposes recommendations at both the user and database-provider levels to improve source-title normalization and strengthen source-level metadata governance, with implications for the accuracy and reproducibility of journal-level retrieval and evaluative uses.

papers.title: Exploring Semantic Table Search in Data Lakes
papers.abstract: Discovery of relevant datasets within data lakes remains a key challenge. Union and join search are effective techniques for discovering data when augmenting an existing table. In exploratory search, instead, keyword search is commonly adopted to find a relatively small set of highly relevant tables matching some search terms. In this context, semantic search is a new technique that exploits the presence of named entities in exemplar tuples used as queries and in target tables. Hence, keyword search and entity search are able to find a diverse set of tables. In this work, we propose \texttt{Thetis++}, which combines keyword and semantic table search to discover relevant tables that combine the semantic signal with the presence of exact keyword matches. Incorporating multiple paradigms and sources of information allow us to combine the best of multiple worlds. Therefore, we study many alternative techniques for combining rankings and evaluate these for the table search task in data lakes. We explore both unsupervised and supervised techniques, including TOPSIS. Finally, alternative to Thetis++ combining keyword and semantic relevance signals, we study a variant of learning-to-rank for the table search task in data lakes. Our evaluation highlights both the limitations of many standard approaches along with some promising directions offered by learned approaches. Furthermore, while indexes for keyword search are quite efficient, here we provide insights into how to improve the scalability of prefiltering techniques for semantic search, comparing LSH indexes with Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds. Our experiments show that HNSW drastically improves the runtime of semantic table search by 4.7X on average whilst retaining the high-quality tables. Together, our findings plot the line for effective and efficient data discovery techniques for semantic data lakes.

papers.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

papers.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
papers.abstract: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.

papers.title: CACO: Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization for Continuous Generative Retrieval
papers.abstract: Continuous generative retrievers powered by flow matching and diffusion sample multiple queries in item embedding space for parallel approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search under fixed retrieval budgets. However, optimizing distribution diversity or target-level interest separation ignores set-level retrieval geometry: sampled queries collapse onto overlapping ANN neighborhoods, while discrete top-K lookup and single-target supervision block end-to-end coverage optimization. We introduce CACO (Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization), a lightweight self-supervised post-training framework that coordinates queries from frozen flow-matching and diffusion retrievers toward complementary item coverage with negligible additional inference latency. CACO uses empirical retrieval frequencies across sampled reference queries as a relevance proxy, formulating a label-free coverage objective that improves recall across all 30 backbone-dataset settings in offline greedy selection experiments. To avoid the inference overhead of generating a large query pool, CACO employs a coordinated query adjustment network that combines inter-query bidirectional attention with gated relative directions, finally updating queries by bounded tangent-space projection and spherical retraction. During training, CACO applies tangential antithetic perturbations and measures each query's marginal gain via counterfactual single-query replacement, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator of smoothed set coverage across non-differentiable ANN search. On eight public benchmarks and an in-house 24-partition streaming industrial dataset, CACO improves Recall@100 by up to 23.7% and Recall@400 by up to 23.9% over the strongest baseline, cuts inter-query overlap by 53.3%-64.9%, and adds only 0.5%-3.0% inference latency.

papers.title: A Task-Level Bias Taxonomy for Historical Image Retrieval
papers.abstract: In recent decades, galleries, libraries, archives, and museums (GLAM institutions) have digitised vast amounts of cultural heritage material, including historical imagery. A major challenge in making these collections publicly accessible is enabling effective search and discovery. Many historical images contain incomplete, sparse, or no descriptive metadata. Consequently, machine learning (ML) methods are increasingly being used to generate or enrich metadata to improve the searchability of such collections. However, artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems can reproduce or amplify existing biases, particularly when applied to historical imagery. Factors such as differences between the data used to train the models and the historical images on which they are applied, degraded image quality, monochrome photographs, and historically biased or incomplete descriptions can reduce model performance and introduce bias into search and retrieval results. In this paper, we examine different forms of bias in historical image collections and review current methods to mitigate them. We investigate how these biases arise and how they influence AI-supported search and retrieval systems.

papers.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
papers.abstract: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.

papers.title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
papers.abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.

papers.title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
papers.abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.

papers.title: Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN
papers.abstract: Graph-based data structures such as DiskANN, HNSW, and NSG constitute the state of the art for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search. Indyk and Xu introduced the notion of $α$-reachable graphs, which include graphs built by DiskANN's slow-preprocessing construction, and proved that greedy search achieves an approximation factor of $\tfrac{α+1}{α-1}$. Independently, Al-Jazzazi et al. proposed adaptive beam search (ABS) with a relaxation parameter $γ> 0$, showing a $\tfrac{2}γ$ approximation on navigable graphs ($α\approx 1$), where greedy search admits no guarantees. In this work, we unify and generalize these results by proving that ABS with parameter $γ$ on $α$-reachable graphs achieves an approximation of $\tfrac{α+1}{α(γ+1)-1}$ for any metric. Moreover, on sorted $α$-reachable graphs (introduced by Gollapudi et al.) under the $\ell_2$ metric, we obtain the tighter bound $\max\bigl(\tfracα{α(γ+1)-1}, \tfrac{α^{2}+1}{α^{2}(γ+1)-1}\bigr)$. Beyond these theoretical results, we design a beam predictor using features inspired by fine-grained analysis of ABS, trained via a constrained objective that minimizes mean distance computations subject to a target recall. On three 100-million-point benchmarks, using graphs built by DiskANN's practical construction, beam predictor lowers mean query latency on SSD-resident indices at matched recall by up to $29.6\%$ relative to classical beam search (CBS). Relative to ABS, it is faster in $11$ of $15$ settings, by up to $6.5\%$, and at most $1.4\%$ slower in the other $4$; at $95\%$ recall, its advantage over ABS grows from $0.8$--$4.2\%$ for $100$ neighbors to $4.6$--$5.6\%$ for $500$ neighbors. In memory, it needs $1.3$--$23.7\%$ fewer distance computations than CBS and $0.0$--$3.9\%$ fewer than ABS.

papers.title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning
papers.abstract: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.

papers.title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

papers.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
papers.abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

papers.title: Explainable Federated Learning via Global-Local Attribution Alignment
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables on-device training without centralizing data, yet existing systems still struggle to provide explanations that are both locally faithful and globally consistent under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints. Prior approaches either keep explanations siloed across clients, transmit heavy or sensitive artifacts, or replace expressive task models with interpretable surrogates that sacrifice accuracy. We propose xFedAlign, a model-agnostic framework that decouples task optimization in parameter space from explanation coordination in a compact group space. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate to produce private, per-class top-k attribution artifacts, which are robustly aggregated by the server into a Global Explanation Prior that softly aligns client explanations without constraining task learning. Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with IID and non-IID partitions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while consistently reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC relative to Local-XAI, FedAttr-Agg, and Fed-XAI, with only a few kilobytes of additional communication per round. Privacy and robustness evaluations further demonstrate reduced membership inference advantage and increased resistance to attribution poisoning, enabling consistent and trustworthy explanations in federated learning.
papers.comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Published in Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)

papers.title: DetouR: Plugging Association Routes into Search Agents for Multi-hop Question Answering
papers.abstract: Search agents answer multi-hop questions by interleaving reasoning with retrieval, deciding at each step what to search next. Existing agents follow semantic routes: they infer what is missing and phrase it as a query, reaching only what the model can name. Yet the decisive page is often one the question never names, frequently just one hyperlink away from evidence already retrieved. Following such association routes reaches more gold pages than semantic search under the same budget. Exploiting them raises two challenges: obtaining the association structure without costly offline graph construction, and keeping linked evidence in the reader's limited context, where relevance- and fusion-based selection discards it. We propose DetouR, a plug-in that reuses the links arriving with retrieved pages and adds no search or LLM call. Link Rerouting replaces near-repeat queries with routes to linked pages, chosen by a lightweight learned scorer; Chain-aware Context Selection runs personalized PageRank over these links so that evidence chains reach the reader intact. Across four agents, DetouR improves EM by 4.0 points on 2Wiki and 1.4 on HotpotQA on average. We also find that heavier LLM models struggle with this non-semantic evidence, adding little over these simple selectors or even falling behind. In summary, our work reveals association routes as a cheap complement to semantic routes that current search agents overlook: added as a plug-in, they improve every agent we test, in replay and in live runs, at no extra search or LLM cost.

papers.title: EchoSpec: Training Search Agents to Weigh Evidence Above Echoes
papers.abstract: Search agents trained with reinforcement learning decide what to retrieve, when to search again, and when to answer. In real corpora, one claim is copied and paraphrased across many pages while the primary source settling a question appears once. We show that reinforcement-learned search agents grant echoes the credence of independent sources and lose their ability to abstain. Across five base models from 3B to 32B and seven released RL agents on multi-hop Wikipedia questions with primary evidence intact, eight paraphrased false-claim echoes overturn 58-73% of previously correct answers, while exact-match RL drives deleted-evidence abstention below 15%. Conditioning on retrieval localizes the failure to evidence acquisition: once primary evidence enters context, agents overrule eight echoes as reliably as one, whereas echoes fill top ranks and halt search early, so larger budgets, forced search turns, or passive passage filtering alone fail to recover displaced evidence. We introduce EchoSpec, specifying reliability across five corpus transformations with known target answers and training in two stages. Verification warm-start teaches multi-hop bridge-entity recovery past echoes, after which group RL optimizes an evidence-gated $λ$-reward with an outcome-independent acquisition bonus and scale-preserving advantages retaining the optimal rule $λ/(1+λ)$. Across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B backbones on nine evaluation suites, EchoSpec cuts eight-echo deference by 30-44 points on Qwen2.5-7B down to 29-31%, nearly quadruples eight-echo reach to 26-27% with zero-shot transfer to unseen BGE and BM25 retrievers, and raises standalone QA precision to 47-55%. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/unihsy/EchoSpec.

papers.title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.
papers.comment: Published in EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 37 pages. Code and data: https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors. Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-main.2372/
